approaches.name: Direct dorsal-radial approach to the radial styloid
approaches.corridor: Anatomic-snuffbox exposure between the first and second extensor compartments

sources.title: Direct Approach To The Radial Styloid
Anatomic considerations when performing the modified Henry approach for exposure of distal radius fractures

procedure_applications.condition: An isolated radial-styloid or radial-column fragment requires direct reduction and fragment-specific fixation

positioning.text: Position supine with the arm on a radiolucent hand table, forearm pronated or neutral, and wrist freely imageable.

setup.text: Map the styloid fragment and planned screw or plate trajectory; prepare magnification and vessel loops for superficial radial nerve and radial artery protection.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark EPL, EPB, APL, the anatomic snuffbox, radial styloid tip, and radial artery pulse.

incision.text: Make a straight incision centered over the anatomic snuffbox and extend proximally or distally only as fracture access requires.

superficial_interval.text: Raise skin-subcutaneous flaps bluntly from retinaculum while identifying and protecting every superficial radial nerve branch.

deep_interval.text: Protect the radial artery across the snuffbox floor, then sharply expose the styloid and elevate first or second compartments only as necessary.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous sensory-nerve plane, extensor retinaculum and compartment interval, periosteum, then radial styloid.

structures_encountered.text: Superficial radial nerve branches, APL, EPB, EPL, radial artery, snuffbox capsule, and styloid fragment are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Superficial radial nerve, radial artery, first- and second-compartment tendons, scapholunate structures, and articular cartilage are at risk.

danger_zones.text: The radial artery crosses the snuffbox floor and sensory branches cross unpredictably in the superficial plane; neither may be treated as a fixed landmark.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid sustained traction on nerve branches or artery and protect extensor tendons from sharp retractors and hardware.

exposure.text: Provides direct access to the radial styloid and radial column for reduction, lag screws, or fragment-specific plating.

limitations.text: Does not expose central, volar-ulnar, or dorsal-ulnar fragments adequately and is unsuitable as the sole approach for complex complete-articular patterns.

extensions.text: Mobilize the first or second extensor compartment or add a separate volar or dorsal approach for other columns rather than stretching the radial corridor.

indications.text: Use for isolated radial-styloid and radial-column fractures needing direct fragment-specific control.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid as an isolated approach when comminution extends beyond the radial column or the snuffbox soft tissues are compromised.

implant_implications.text: Place screws or plate under direct visualization while avoiding radiocarpal penetration and irritation of first- or second-compartment tendons.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use PA, lateral, oblique, and tangential views to verify styloid reduction, screw length, and joint containment.

closure.text: Confirm artery flow and tendon glide, repair retinacular tissue as needed, and close without trapping superficial radial nerve branches.

complications.text: Complications include radial sensory neuritis or neuroma, radial-artery injury, tendon irritation or rupture, joint penetration, stiffness, and symptomatic hardware.

bailouts.text: Add a column-specific exposure if reduction remains unseen; do not enlarge blindly around the radial artery or sensory nerve branches.

questions.question: What forms the snuffbox boundaries?
questions.answer: EPL dorsally and APL/EPB volarly, with the radial styloid and scaphoid in the floor.

questions.question: Which two structures require explicit protection?
questions.answer: The superficial radial nerve branches and radial artery.

questions.question: Which compartments may be elevated?
questions.answer: The first and second extensor compartments.

approaches.name: Dorsal approach for wrist-spanning bridge plate
approaches.region: dorsal wrist, distal radius, and third metacarpal
approaches.corridor: Third extensor-compartment release with radial EPL transposition and subperiosteal elevation of the intact fourth compartment

sources.title: Dorsal Approach For Joint Spanning Plate
Dorsal Bridge Plate for Distal Radius Fractures: A Systematic Review
Systematic review: dorsal bridge plating in distal radius fractures

procedure_applications.condition: A highly comminuted intra-articular fracture needs internal wrist-spanning fixation or the patient requires a durable load-sharing construct
A dorsal spanning exposure is required for wrist fusion

positioning.text: Position supine with arm on a radiolucent hand table, forearm pronated, and elbow and shoulder accessible for traction and imaging.

setup.text: Template plate length and metacarpal choice, plan proximal and distal windows and tendon-safe tunnel, and counsel that planned plate removal is usually required.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark Lister tubercle, EPL course, third metacarpal, wrist joint, radial shaft, and superficial radial nerve territory.

incision.text: Use aligned dorsal windows over distal radius and third metacarpal, extending the central exposure as needed for third-compartment release.

superficial_interval.text: Mobilize flaps carefully to protect superficial radial nerve branches and identify extensor compartments before tunneling.

deep_interval.text: Open the third compartment in line with EPL without cutting it, transpose EPL radially, and elevate the intact fourth compartment subperiosteally toward the third metacarpal.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous nerve plane, extensor retinaculum, third-compartment sheath, subperiosteal fourth-compartment plane, then radius and third metacarpal.

structures_encountered.text: EPL, EDC/EIP compartment, second compartment when mobilized, dorsal capsule, radius, and third metacarpal are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: EPL and other extensor tendons, superficial radial nerve, posterior interosseous nerve distally, dorsal sensory branches, and articular surfaces are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Confirm the plate lies deep to tendons without trapping EPL or fourth-compartment tendons and avoid blind passage off bone.

retraction_hazards.text: Use vessel-loop control of EPL without excessive traction and avoid crushing the intact fourth compartment against retractors or plate.

exposure.text: Provides a dorsal internal-fixator corridor from radial shaft across wrist to third metacarpal and can expose the intermediate column.

limitations.text: Temporarily sacrifices wrist motion, usually requires removal, and may not directly reduce all articular fragments without adjunct windows.

extensions.text: Mobilize second compartment radially or extend radius/metacarpal windows for direct plate seating and fragment-specific adjunct fixation.

indications.text: Use for severely comminuted intra-articular fractures, poor distal fixation stock, selected polytrauma load-bearing needs, or wrist fusion.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid when a nonspanning construct can reliably restore anatomy and motion, or dorsal soft tissue and tendon conditions cannot tolerate the plate.

implant_implications.text: Seat the bridge plate deep to tendons on radius and third metacarpal, restore length by ligamentotaxis without overdistraction, and plan later removal.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm radial length, inclination, tilt, articular alignment, metacarpal and radial screw length, and absence of overdistraction.

closure.text: Verify tendon glide and plate coverage, leave EPL safely transposed as planned, repair retinacular intervals without constriction, and close in layers.

complications.text: Complications include tendon adhesion or rupture, digital stiffness, hardware failure, infection, nonunion or malunion, pain, and planned reoperation for removal.

bailouts.text: Open an additional window if the plate cannot pass on bone or tendons cannot be protected; add fragment-specific fixation when ligamentotaxis is insufficient.

questions.question: Which compartment is opened completely?
questions.answer: The third extensor compartment containing EPL.

questions.question: How is the fourth compartment handled?
questions.answer: It is elevated subperiosteally while kept intact.

questions.question: What major treatment tradeoff should be discussed?
questions.answer: Temporary wrist immobilization and a planned second operation for plate removal.

approaches.name: Modified Henry volar approach to the distal radius
approaches.corridor: Through FCR sheath, ulnar to radial artery, then between FPL and radial artery to pronator quadratus

sources.title: Anatomic considerations when performing the modified Henry approach for exposure of distal radius fractures
Relative Effectiveness of Surgical Treatment Options for Distal Radius Fractures

procedure_applications.condition: Most volar-displaced or reducible distal-radius fractures require volar plate fixation

positioning.text: Position supine with arm on radiolucent hand table, forearm supinated, and wrist extended over a small support.

setup.text: Mark FCR and radial artery, review lunate-facet and watershed-line anatomy, and prepare carpal-tunnel decompression as a separate or extensile option when indicated.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark FCR tendon, radial styloid, wrist crease, radial artery pulse, scaphoid tubercle, and palmaris longus when present.

incision.text: Incise longitudinally along the radial border of FCR, tailored to fracture and plate length.

superficial_interval.text: Open FCR sheath and retract tendon ulnarly while protecting the palmar cutaneous median-nerve branch on the ulnar side.

deep_interval.text: Develop between FPL and radial artery, sweep FPL ulnarly, and elevate pronator quadratus with an L-shaped incision whose distal limb stays near the watershed line.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous palmar-cutaneous nerve plane, FCR sheath, FPL-radial artery interval, pronator quadratus and periosteum, then volar radius.

structures_encountered.text: FCR, radial artery, palmar cutaneous median-nerve branch, FPL, pronator quadratus, volar capsule, and distal radius are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Palmar cutaneous median-nerve branch, median nerve proximally, radial artery, FPL, flexor tendons, and radiocarpal capsule are at risk.

danger_zones.text: The palmar cutaneous branch is most vulnerable distally and median nerve proximity increases proximally; remain in the defined FCR-based interval.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid prolonged radial-artery traction and excessive ulnar retraction of FPL and median nerve; use broad atraumatic retractors.

exposure.text: Exposes most volar distal-radius fractures and supports volar plate placement; it does not directly decompress the carpal tunnel.

limitations.text: Isolated lunate-facet, dorsal rim, and highly complex high-energy patterns may need ulnar-volar, dorsal, or combined approaches.

extensions.text: Extend proximally along FCR or add a separate carpal-tunnel, ulnar-volar, or dorsal exposure according to pathology.

indications.text: Use for most operatively treated distal-radius fractures amenable to volar reduction and plating.

relative_contraindications.text: Choose an alternative or combined approach when the critical fragment cannot be controlled volarly or volar skin is compromised.

implant_implications.text: Position the plate proximal to the watershed line when possible and confirm distal screws support subchondral bone without joint or dorsal-tendon penetration.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use PA, lateral, oblique, dorsal tangential, and tilted views to assess reduction, watershed position, and every distal screw.

closure.text: Reapproximate pronator quadratus over the plate when feasible, close FCR sheath only without trapping the palmar cutaneous nerve, then close skin.

complications.text: Complications include median or palmar-cutaneous neuropathy, radial-artery injury, flexor or extensor tendon irritation or rupture, joint penetration, stiffness, and hardware prominence.

bailouts.text: Add the required column-specific exposure when reduction remains unseen and decompress the carpal tunnel through an appropriate separate or extensile route when indicated.

questions.question: What is the defining interval?
questions.answer: Between FCR and the radial artery, with the approach ulnar to the artery.

questions.question: Which nerve branch is at risk distally?
questions.answer: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve.

questions.question: Where is the distal pronator-quadratus limb placed?
questions.answer: At the watershed line a few millimeters proximal to the joint.
